steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Zakah is the third Pillar of Islam — Muslims must give 2.5% of their surplus wealth each year to charity. It is not optional; it is a religious duty and a form of worship. Shi'a Muslims also pay khums (20% of surplus income) to their religious leaders.

steps.title: RS Exam Tips — Zakah and Khums
steps.body: 1. For Zakah and Khums questions, always include specific scriptural or source references where relevant 2. Explain both religious and non-religious viewpoints 3. Use specialist vocabulary precisely (e.g. terms from the specification) 4. Evaluate by analysing strengths and weaknesses of different views before reaching your conclusion 5. Link your discussion of Zakah and Khums to its real-world impact on believers and society

steps.title: UK Context
steps.body: If a British Muslim has savings of £20,000 held for a full year above the nisab threshold, they would pay £500 in zakah (2.5% of £20,000). Islamic Relief UK and the National Zakat Foundation provide online zakah calculators to help British Muslims calculate their obligation accurately.

steps.title: UK Context
steps.body: In the UK, Shi’a mosques and centres such as the Al-Khoei Foundation in London and the Imam Ali Foundation collect and distribute khums according to the guidance of their marja. These funds support religious schools, community programmes and charitable work both in Britain and internationally.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain two reasons why zakah is important for Muslims.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: 1) Zakah purifies wealth — by giving away 2.5% of their surplus, Muslims acknowledge that all wealth ultimately belongs to Allah and they are merely its stewards. Hoarding wealth is condemned in the Q

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always refer to specific sources of authority (scripture, sacred texts, religious leaders) Explain contrasting beliefs — different views within and between traditions Use key terminology precisely (e.g. tawhid, atonement, sanctity of life) For 12-mark evaluation questions, consider both sides before reaching a justified conclusion Link beliefs to their impact on individuals, communities and society Acknowledge diversity — no religious tradition has a single, uniform view
